title: Mixture-of-Memory Embeddings for Context-Aware Sparse Lookup
claim: Prior lookups map a token's surface form to one fixed entry; ours gates over hidden state to read context-dependent memory.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; example box, block stack, zoomed block detail
description: The figure has three parts. At left, a boxed panel shows two sentences using the word 'bug', one tagged 'insect' and one tagged 'software', with 'bug' highlighted. Below them, three methods are listed: VE/STEM gives id(bug) for both senses, Engram gives hash(of a bug) and hash(to a bug), and Ours gives f(bug), g_θ(h¹) and f(bug), g_θ(h²). In the centre is a vertical stack of an embedding layer, a transformer block and a purple memory-augmented transformer block, topped by an LM head. A '×N' loop wraps the stack. Dotted lines zoom the memory-augmented block into the right panel. That panel shows Q/K/V projections, grouped query attention and feed forward, with residual plus signs. A memory router and a gate read a memory table of idle (grey) and activated (coloured) slots and inject the result into the value stream. Purple marks the memory components, blue the standard transformer parts.
caption: Left: the same token can carry different senses, and prior token-indexed methods (VE/STEM, canonical Engram) commit each row to a single fixed memory while \ours{} dispatches to different slots depending on the hidden state (see Figure [ref] and Section [ref] for the learned routing). Right: \ours{} alternates regular transformer blocks with memory-augmented blocks; in each memory-augmented block, a context-aware router retrieves a memory vector and injects it into the attention value stream.
abstract: Scaling large language models efficiently has motivated sparse capacity mechanisms such as Mixture-of-Experts and, more recently, conditional memory: token-indexed embedding tables that augment the backbone with cheap parametric lookups. Existing memory-embedding methods retrieve via a deterministic function of the surface form, which collapses different contextual senses of the same token (e.g., python the language vs. the animal) into a single fixed entry. We introduce Mixture of Memory Embeddings (MoME), a context-aware memory mechanism that replaces each token's single memory row with a mixture of M slots and uses a learned gate over the hidden state to choose which slots to read at each position. In controlled pretraining experiments across nanochat, Llama-3/MobileLLM, and Qwen3 backbones, MoME improves over Value Embedding, Bigram, and STEM baselines in iso-parameter and iso-training-FLOP settings, shows a more promising memory-size scaling trend at sub-billion scale, and remains efficient in training and inference. Qualitative routing analyses on polysemous tokens further suggest that the learned mixture exhibits a degree of semantic interpretability, dispatching the same surface token to distinct memory slots under different senses.
